item.title: Clinical Case Scenario
item.description:
Clinical Case Scenario

A 28-year-old female with a history of mild anxiety presents to the outpatient cardiology clinic for a routine evaluation after being told she had a “heart murmur” during a physical exam for a new job. She is generally asymptomatic but reports occasional episodes of sharp, localized chest pain and palpitations that are unrelated to physical exertion.

Physical Examination: Vital Signs: BP 118/76 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, RR 14 breaths/min. Cardiovascular: On auscultation at the apex, there is a mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur. Dynamic Auscultation: * When the patient stands up from a squatting position, the click occurs earlier in systole and the murmur becomes longer and louder. When the patient performs a squatting maneuver, the click moves later into systole and the murmur decreases in intensity. Musculoskeletal: The patient has a slender build with relatively long fingers (arachnodactyly) and mild pectus excavatum. Laboratory Investigations: ECG: Normal sinus rhythm with occasional premature ventricular contractions (PVCs). Transthoracic Echocardiography (TTE): M-mode/2D: Shows superior displacement of the posterior mitral valve leaflet into the left atrium during systole ($>2$ mm beyond the mitral annular plane). Morphology: The leaflets appear thickened ($>5$ mm) and redundant, consistent with myxomatous degeneration. Color Doppler: Trace to mild mitral regurgitation is noted. What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
